In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the PCAT provides a standardized and valid assessment of candidates’ abilities to apply their pre-pharmacy knowledge and skills to the cognitive tasks required of pharmacists.

the PCAT is a valid, reliable, and useful measure of candidates’ abilities to identify, interpret, analyze, and evaluate information assumed to have covered in pre-pharmaceutical science, math, biology, chemistry, physics, and general education courses.
the PCAT is not a measure of intelligence or a measure of a candidate’s ability to learn.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PCAT scores are not only measures of knowledge but are also indicators of candidates’ abilities to apply their knowledge to new situations and to think critically.
candidates’ PCAT scores are not simply measures of “how smart” they are.

PCAT subtest scaled scores and percentile rank scores provide information about candidates’ performances on the cognitive tasks that are assumed to have been learned in pre-pharmacy coursework and that PCAT writing scores reflect the candidates’ ability to communicate their ideas in writing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PCAT subtest scaled scores and percentile rankings do not reflect the same thing.
PCAT scores are best interpreted in the context of candidates’ educational and experiential backgrounds and not as absolute, objective measures of their abilities.
candidates’ PCAT scores reflect their ability to identify and interpret information, to analyze and evaluate that information, to make inferences and predictions, and to communicate their findings.
